contributions.headingText: Fibrin-associated large B-cell lymphoma (FA-LBCL) is a neoplasm of large B cells found incidentally at sites of chronic fibrin deposition in confined natural or acquired anatomical spaces and sites.
2A81.Y & XH0RM6 Other specified diffuse large B-cell lymphomas & Fibrin-associated EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Acceptable: fibrin-associated diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

Not recommended: microscopic/incidental diffuse large B-cell lymphoma associated with chronic inflammation; EBV-positive large B-cell lymphoma arising in atrial myxoma; microscopic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma occurring in pseudocyst.

FA-LBCL arises in sites of chronic fibrin deposition including cyst and pseudocyst cavities {22472958}, in the peri-implant space of breast implants {31753922}, and in chronic haematomas {31519155}, as well as in intravascular or intracardiac locations, such as the surface of cardiac myxomas {28195879}, endovascular grafts, and prosthetic cardiac valves {20139760} (see #30416Table 4.34). Embolization of fibrinous material from intravascular or cardiac sites involved by FA-LBCL may carry the lymphoma cells along with the embolus {28195879}.

The clinical presentation depends on the underlying anatomical lesion involved by FA-LBCL and can be asymptomatic. Some patients with FA-LBCL in atrial myxoma or endovascular grafts present with thromboembolic events; however, it is unknown whether the risk of thromboembolism differs from similar vascular grafts or myxomas without FA-LBCL.

The overall incidence is unknown. FA-LBCL is diagnosed in adults, with a wide age range (25–91 years; median: 59.5 years). Some anatomical localizations of the disease (breast-implant associated, testicular haematoma-associated) have an obvious sex bias (see #30416Table 4.34).
The etiology is unknown. Patients rarely have evidence of recognized immunosuppression, with the possible exception of immunosenescence.

FA-LBCL is associated with EBV infection, but rare EBV-negative cases have also been described {31863183; 33913371}. The local microenvironment is hypothesized to create a form of local immune escape excluding EBV+ B cells from immunosurveillance {20062008}. Dense fibrin around the tumour cells, upregulation of PDL1 {28195879}, and production of IL-6 by cardiac myxomas have been implicated in creating a permissive environment {25307939}. FA-LBCL is usually negative for rearrangements of BCL2, BCL6, and MYC, but rare cases with BCL6 or MYC rearrangement have been reported {28782131; 32110798}.

Aggregates of large lymphoid cells, often of atypical immunoblastic type, are surrounded by fibrin and cellular debris. There may be focal infiltration of myxomatous stroma (e.g. in cardiac myxoma) or fibrous capsular tissue (e.g. in breast implant–associated cases) but infiltration into pre-existing normal parenchymal tissue or mass formation is absent. Mitotic figures and apoptotic changes are frequent. Associated inflammation is usually sparse, although a prominent lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate may be found in some cases {28195879}. Rare EBV-negative cases have a presentation and histology identical to those of the EBV-positive cases {31863183; 33913371}.

Immunohistochemistry

The immunophenotype usually resembles activated B cells: the tumour cells are positive for pan–B-cell markers (CD20, CD79a, and PAX5). CD10 is negative. IRF4 (MUM1) is positive. BCL2, BCL6, and CD30 are variable. A minority have plasmablastic features, including intracytoplasmic positivity for monotypic light chain, positive CD138, and decreased expression of CD20 and PAX5. Aberrant expression of T-cell markers, typically CD3, CD4, or CD43, is occasionally present. Ki-67/MIB1 staining shows a high proliferation index, usually > 90%. Most cases have type III EBV latency, signified by positivity for LMP1 and EBNA2 and negativity for BZLF1 {28195879}. KSHV/HHV8 (by latency-associated nuclear antigen [LANA] immunohistochemistry) is negative.

Differential diagnosis

The lack of mass formation and infiltrative growth distinguishes this entity from EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) and DLBCL associated with chronic inflammation.
Lymphoma cells are large with narrow to broad basophilic cytoplasm and round or irregular nuclei with coarse chromatin. Diagnosis of FA-LBCL is not possible from cytological material alone.
In situ hybridization for EBV-encoded small RNA (EBER) is nearly always positive.

Essential: microscopic aggregates of atypical large B lymphocytes in a background of fibrinous debris; presentation at sites of chronic fibrin deposition in confined natural or acquired anatomical spaces and sites; no mass-forming lymphoma lesion; no infiltration into pre-existing normal parenchymal tissue.

Desirable: non–germinal-centre B-cell immunophenotype; EBV positivity.
All reported cases have been localized to a single extranodal site, consistent with stage IE of the Lugano classification {25113753}.

No cases of biopsy-proven FA-LBCL with subsequent development of infiltrative or disseminated lymphoma have been identified so far. Retrospective reports show no difference in outcomes between patients treated with chemotherapy, chemoimmunotherapy, or surgical excision {28195879}. No deaths directly attributable to FA-LBCL have been reported {28195879; 28782131; 31519155}. When the underlying lesion cannot be completed excised, persistence or local regrowth of FA-LBCL has been reported {24060945; 28195879}.
